title: Sonu Nigam Admits He Uses Auto-Tune in Some Songs, Blames Digitised Recording
excerpt: The veteran singer, long considered one of the few Bollywood vocalists who never needed pitch correction, said digital recording environments make a raw voice sound off without some processing.
body:
• Sonu Nigam has admitted to using auto-tune in certain songs, breaking from his long-held reputation as a singer who never needed pitch correction.
  • The singer blamed the shift from live instrumentation to digitised recording, saying a raw voice can sound off in modern studio environments.
  • Fellow artists including Arijit Singh and composer Rochak Kohli had previously singled out Nigam as a rare exception who didn't need auto-tune.
  • Nigam's comments come amid a broader industry conversation about the role of technology in Indian music production.

Sonu Nigam, one of Indian cinema's most celebrated playback singers, has admitted that he uses auto-tune in some of his recordings — a candid confession that challenges the long-standing perception of him as one of the few Bollywood vocalists who never needed the technology.

In an interview reported by the Times of India and Hindustan Times, Nigam explained that the shift from live instrumentation to digitised recording has fundamentally changed how a voice sounds in the studio. He noted that in the earlier era of live recording, instruments like the sarangi and strings were played alongside the singer, creating a natural warmth that complemented the human voice. In today's digitised environments, however, a completely raw voice can sound off, he said.

"Voice sounds off if it's raw."

— Sonu Nigam, on why auto-tune is sometimes necessary in digital recordings

Breaking a Long-Held Image

For years, Nigam has been held up as the gold standard of natural vocal ability in Bollywood. Fellow singer Arijit Singh, in a widely discussed conversation on The Music Podcast, specifically named Nigam as the only singer who "can't go out of tune." Composer Rochak Kohli similarly stated that "Sonu Nigam, Shreya Ghoshal and a selected few do not need auto-tuners."

Even casual industry observers have associated Nigam with vocal purity. In a past interview, actress Amyra Dastur told SpotboyE that she loved the song "Abhi Mujh Mein Kahin" because "it does not sound auto-tuned. In any case, I don't think Sonu sir uses that software."

Nigam's admission doesn't contradict his vocal ability but reframes the conversation around modern music production. His point is not that his voice has weakened but that the recording medium itself has changed — and with it, the tools required to deliver a polished product.

The Auto-Tune Debate in Bollywood

Auto-tune has been a quietly contentious topic in the Indian music industry for years. AR Rahman is widely credited with introducing the technology to Indian recordings in a subtle, tasteful way, according to Arijit Singh. Some composers like Mithoon Sharma and Vishal Bhardwaj avoid it entirely, while others like Pritam Chakraborty use it regularly to enhance sound quality, Singh noted in his Music Podcast interview.

Nigam himself has previously spoken about how technology has reshaped the industry. In an earlier interview reported by Bollywood Life, he observed that digital tools have created more singers but fewer legends. "Earlier, singers like Lataji and Ashaji used to sing their songs in one take. The whole song used to be recorded from start to finish," he said. "But now anyone whose texture of voice is good is getting a chance to become a singer."

A Career at 30 Years

The admission comes at a moment when Nigam's career is hitting new milestones. He received the 40th Lata Mangeshkar Award in September 2025, describing it as "a sign of encouragement and blessing." He launched the "I Believe Your Music" initiative on World Music Day 2026 to mentor emerging independent artists. His world tour, "The Revolution," celebrating 30 years in music, kicks off at Abu Dhabi's Etihad Arena on August 21.

On the broader question of technology in music, Nigam has maintained a balanced stance. Speaking about AI's growing role, he said in an interview with The Indian Express: "AI should be treated as an assistant, not as your boss. It should never replace the human soul that gives music its true essence."

What It Means for the Industry

Nigam's candor is likely to open up a more honest conversation about production practices in Bollywood music. If even the singer most associated with natural pitch perfection acknowledges using auto-tune, it normalizes the tool as a production standard rather than a crutch. For listeners and younger artists, the message is clear: technology in music isn't about hiding weakness — it's about adapting to a changed recording landscape.
nri_angle: Sonu Nigam is among the most recognizable voices for the Indian diaspora, whose songs define nostalgia for NRIs worldwide; his candid take on auto-tune reshapes perceptions of a singer who has been a cultural constant across three decades.
